```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.6)
```

lunarcast forecasts monthly and quarterly series that react to **moving
holidays**: holidays such as Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha, the Chinese New Year
or Easter, whose Gregorian date changes every year. This vignette walks
through a complete analysis. The method is explained in
`vignette("theory")` and compared with the classical calendar variation model
in `vignette("classic-vs-lunarcast")`.

## Installation

```r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("novrisuhermi/lunarcast")

# or, with vignettes
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("novrisuhermi/lunarcast", build_vignettes = TRUE)
```

## The data

The package contains `sapi`, the monthly Google Trends index for "sapi"
(cattle) in Indonesia. Interest peaks before Eid al-Adha, when cattle are
bought for the sacrifice.

```{r data, message = FALSE}
library(lunarcast)
plot(sapi, xlab = "", ylab = "Google Trends index",
     main = "Search interest in \"sapi\"")
```

Two features make this series hard: the peaks move to an earlier month every
few years, and their size changes, from almost nothing in 2004 to more than
three times the usual level in the late 2010s.

## Step 1: holiday dates

```{r dates}
adha <- holiday_dates("idul_adha")
tail(adha, 4)
```

`holiday_dates()` gives the Indonesian dates of Eid al-Adha, Eid al-Fitr and
the Chinese New Year from 2004 to 2027, and `easter_dates()` computes Easter
and the holidays that follow from it. Any other holiday is simply a vector
of dates.

```{r other-dates}
easter_dates(2025:2026, offset = -2)   # Good Friday
my_holiday <- as.Date(c("2024-03-11", "2025-03-29", "2026-03-19"))
```

## Step 2: from dates to regressors

A holiday influences the days around it, not a calendar month.
`holiday_window()` computes the share of a window of days around each
occurrence that falls in each month.

```{r window}
w <- holiday_window(adha, window = c(-3, 7), y = sapi)
window(w, start = c(2020, 6), end = c(2020, 9))
```

Eid al-Adha fell on 31 July 2020. The window from three days before to seven
days after puts 36% of the holiday in July and 64% in August, where the
searches indeed peaked. A monthly dummy would have put everything in July.
You do not need to build these regressors yourself; `lunarcast()` does it and
chooses the window.

## Step 3: fit the automatic model

```{r fit}
hol <- list(adha  = holiday_dates("idul_adha"),
            fitri = holiday_dates("idul_fitri"))
fit <- lunarcast(sapi, hol)
fit
```

How to read the output:

* The first line is the fitted regression with ARIMA errors and its AICc.
* `Structure` is the trend and seasonal structure chosen by
  cross-validation; `CV-RMSE (SE)` lists all candidates with their
  cross-validated error and its standard error. The default one-SE rule takes
  the simplest structure within one standard error of the best.
* For each holiday you see whether its effect is `constant` or `two-level`,
  the selected window in days around the holiday and, for two-level effects,
  the level-2 rule used to forecast the next effect.
* `ratio` is the multiplicative effect $e^{\alpha}$: 2.5 means that the
  holiday (when its whole window falls in one month) multiplies the level of
  that month by 2.5.

## Step 4: inspect the holiday effects

```{r effects}
eff <- holiday_effects(fit)
head(eff, 4)
plot(fit)
```

Each point is the effect of one Eid al-Adha with its 95% confidence interval;
the open circle is the forecast for the next occurrence. The effect grew until
the late 2010s and has declined since, which a single constant effect cannot
represent.

## Step 5: forecast

```{r forecast}
fc <- forecast(fit, h = 13)
plot(fc, include = 60)
fc$future_effects
round(cbind(forecast = fc$mean, lower = fc$lower[, 1],
            upper = fc$upper[, 1]), 1)
```

The forecast is the median on the original scale with a 95% interval that
includes the uncertainty about the next holiday effect.
`fc$future_effects` shows the effect used for each new occurrence and the rule
that produced it.

### Scenarios

To ask "what if the next Eid al-Adha doubles the level?", fix its effect:

```{r scenario}
sc <- forecast(fit, h = 13, level2 = list(adha = log(2)))
round(cbind(model = fc$mean, scenario = sc$mean)[5:7, ], 1)
```

## Taking control of the automatic choices

Every automatic choice can be fixed, which also makes fitting much faster.

| Argument | What it controls | Example |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `window` | days around each holiday | `window = list(adha = c(-3, 7), fitri = c(-28, 3))` |
| `effect` | constant or two-level effect | `effect = list(adha = "two-level", fitri = "constant")` |
| `trend`, `season` | trend and seasonal structure | `trend = "stochastic", season = "none"` |
| `select` | how the structure is chosen | `select = "aicc"` |
| `cv_rule`, `cv_years` | cross-validation rule and origins | `cv_rule = "min", cv_years = 3` |
| `level2` | rule for future effects | `level2 = list(adha = "rw")` |
| `outliers` | detect AO, LS and TC outliers | `outliers = TRUE` |
| `lambda` | transformation (`0` = log) | `lambda = NULL` for additive effects |

```{r fixed}
fast <- lunarcast(sapi, hol,
                  window = list(adha = c(-3, 7), fitri = c(-28, 3)),
                  effect = list(adha = "two-level", fitri = "constant"),
                  trend = "stochastic", season = "none")
fast
```

## The classical model

The classical calendar variation model, with a dummy for the holiday month
and the same effect every year, is available in the six structures m1 to m6:

```{r classic}
m6 <- calvar_classic(sapi, adha, trend = "stochastic", season = "stochastic")
m6
```

`calvar_classic_all()` fits all six at once, and `forecast()` works for both
kinds of models. The two approaches are compared in
`vignette("classic-vs-lunarcast")`.

## Evaluating forecasts

`rolling_origin()` refits models at the end of every year and forecasts the
next year; `rolling_summary()` reports the RMSE overall, in holiday months, in
years in which the holiday moved to another month, and the median of the
yearly RMSEs.

```{r rolling, eval = FALSE}
models <- list(
  classic_m6 = function(y, h)
    forecast(calvar_classic(y, adha, "stochastic", "stochastic"), h = h)$mean,
  lunarcast  = function(y, h) forecast(lunarcast(y, hol), h = h)$mean
)
r <- rolling_origin(sapi, adha, models, first = 2012)
rolling_summary(r)
```

`forecast_accuracy()` gives RMSE, MAE, MAPE and sMAPE for a single test
period.
